nameStory: The striped barnacle gets its name from the distinctive stripes or bands that often decorate its cone-shaped shell. It's also called the purple acorn barnacle for the purplish hues that can tint its shell, and Amphitrite's rock barnacle after the sea goddess Amphitrite from Greek mythology.
description: Striped barnacles are small, cone-shaped marine animals that cement themselves permanently to hard surfaces underwater. These aren't mollusks like you might expect, but are actually crustaceans - relatives of crabs and lobsters that have evolved to live upside-down in a protective shell fortress. They typically grow to about the size of a nickel or smaller, forming crusty colonies that can cover rocks, pilings, and boat hulls. Inside their volcano-like shells, they filter feed by extending feathery legs to catch tiny particles from the water.

idTips.label: Striped shell pattern
idTips.description: Look for distinctive stripes, bands, or radiating lines on the cone-shaped shell that give this species its common name - these markings are often purple, brown, or reddish against a lighter background

idTips.label: Cone shape
idTips.description: The shell forms a classic volcano or cone shape when viewed from the side, feeling rough and crusty to the touch like barnacle-encrusted sandpaper

idTips.label: Purple coloration
idTips.description: Many individuals show purplish tints in their shells, especially along the stripe patterns, which can range from subtle lavender to deep purple-brown

idTips.label: Size and clustering
idTips.description: Individual barnacles are typically nickel-sized or smaller, often growing in dense clusters that create a bumpy, crusty texture covering surfaces

idTips.label: Feathery feeding appendages
idTips.description: When underwater and actively feeding, you can see delicate, feathery leg-like structures called cirri extending and retracting from the shell opening like tiny underwater flowers

habitat: In New England's warmer coastal waters, striped barnacles attach to rocky intertidal zones, pier pilings, boat hulls, and other hard underwater surfaces. They prefer areas with good water circulation and are more commonly found in harbors and protected bays rather than exposed outer coastlines. Look for them in the lower intertidal zone where they remain submerged most of the time.

seasonality.spring: Young barnacles begin settling and growing on surfaces as waters warm, appearing as tiny white specks that gradually develop their characteristic striped patterns.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when barnacles are most active in feeding and reproduction, with mature individuals showing their best coloration and stripe patterns.
seasonality.fall: Barnacles continue feeding actively in still-warm waters, building up reserves before winter while maintaining their distinct markings.
seasonality.winter: Growth slows significantly in cold water, but established colonies persist through winter, with shells appearing more weathered and less colorful.

funFact: Barnacles are actually upside-down crustaceans that kick food into their mouths with their feet - they cement their heads to rocks and use their legs like tiny fishing nets to catch plankton!
confusionNotes: Striped barnacles can be confused with other acorn barnacles, but their distinctive striped or banded shell pattern sets them apart from the more uniform coloration of most other species. Remember: if you see stripes, especially with purple tints, you're likely looking at a striped barnacle.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their shell-like appearance, barnacles are crustaceans, not mollusks - they're actually more closely related to crabs and shrimp than to clams or oysters, which explains why they have jointed legs instead of the muscular foot that true shellfish possess.
compareHints: Striped barnacles are distinguished from their Amphibalanus relatives by their prominent striped shell patterns - Bay Barnacles tend to be more uniformly colored, while Ivory Barnacles are typically white or cream-colored without the distinctive banding. The purple coloration often present in Striped Barnacles is also a helpful distinguishing feature from the generally lighter-colored shells of other species in this genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Bay barnacles differ from their close relatives by their preference for brackish water and their distinctive diamond-shaped opening.
Compared to its close relatives, Amphibalanus venustus is typically more perfectly cone-shaped and symmetrical than the Bay Barnacle, which tends to be more irregular and compressed.
Ivory barnacles are distinguished from their close relatives by their exceptionally smooth, white shells.
Compared to its relatives in New England, this species is distinguished by its chalky white color and relatively small size.
